en: The horse herder out on the ridge,
Mounting his stallion and beating it,
Came out too from one side.
Raising the battle cry, “Manas!”
His stallion would not go, flopping along.
When he reached the middle,
What could the poor stallion rider do?
He could not catch up, flapping along.
Good heavens, all the ridges rang with shouts!
The shepherds out on the ridges,
Throwing their staffs into the air,
They too went shouting,
Raising the battle cry, “Manas!”
Their anti-slip foot blocks clattering,
What could the poor men on foot do?
They too could not catch up, flopping along.
There is more wonder yet!
All the desert rang with shouting.
The cowherds out in the desert,
Mounting their bulls and beating them,
These poor men came out too,
Raising the battle cry, “Manas!”
What could the poor bull riders do?
The bulls would not go, flapping along.
When they reached the middle,
The poor men could go no farther, flopping along.
All the plains rang with shouting.
The reaper out on the plain,
Throwing his sickle into the air,
Running on foot with heavy strides,
Shouting from the side,
This poor man came out too,
Raising the battle cry, “Manas!”
“Countless gold and many gold coins—
It is the horse of the woman who scattered them!
As a widow to Bukhara,
It is the horse of the woman who fled!
Drive on, drive on! It is Manas's horse!
God, it is Manas's horse!
Hunched up like a taigan hound,
It is the horse of my sister who trotted along!
Fleeing Talas, wandering on foot,
It is the horse of my sister who came!”
Throwing his sickle into the air,
Running on foot with heavy strides,
The poor reaper lumbered along,
He too could not catch up, flopping along.
All the lowlands rang with shouting.
Everyone on the plain
Raising the battle cry, “Manas!”
O Lord, all the mountains rang with shouts!
Everyone in the mountains
Raised the battle cry, “Manas!”
Lowlands and mountains rang with shouting.
O Lord, all the lowlands and mountains
Raised the battle cry, “Manas!”
To the city of Bukhara,
Taytoru came in first.
When he reached twelve years of age,
The young lord Semetey,
The many prizes in Bukhara,
Swept them all up.
Great treasure, countless possessions,
There were a thousand dark camels,
A thousand black mares with white blazes.
Gold was weighed out in poods as prizes,
Bales of costly telegey cloth were offered.
To those who knew, it was Manas's memorial feast.
Seven houses filled with treasure,
Livestock was offered with reckless abundance.
To the city of Bukhara,
Taytoru came in first.
The many prizes in Bukhara,
He swept them all up.
The people of eight khans gathered.
Around them was a grove of plane trees.
Amid those plane trees,
Though soaked in water forty years,
Its surface would not fade a trace.
Though left in water eighty years,
It would not shake loose and rot.
The carpet patterned in gold—
Upon it was a golden throne.
To Bukhara's golden throne,
The eight khans sent word.
All the many prizes,
The boy swept them all up.
Putting my golden crown upon him,
Seating him on the golden throne,
Saying “Amen,” the boy
They raised as khan.
For the little one at twelve,
There would be no regret even in death.
For the little one left by Manas,
No one capable of resisting remained.
In Bukhara of the seven gates,
See how the boy Semetey grew,
How he became a giant!
Taytoru's many prizes,
Not letting anyone catch his tail,
The young lord Semetey—
See how he became their master!
Taytoru's prizes,
When he had swept them all up,
“What of your promise, lord?” they said.
Some sixty wrestlers,
When they stood in a row,
Faithful to his promise, true to one word,
The only son of the mighty khan,
To all his wrestlers,
He agreed to what they said.
Among some sixty wrestlers,
The many prizes in Bukhara,
He divided them equally.
“He put not a coin in his pocket,
Took not half a length of calico as booty.
Truly created by God,
Did you see that he is His servant?
Of poor Sultan Manas,
Did you see that he is the son?
His first ancestor was Tugol Khan,
From the beginning touched by Kydyr,
Offspring of a firmly rooted lineage,
His early ancestors all were khans,
Offspring of a sovereign.
His stock is the dear Kyrgyz people.
His father Manas was an exceptional lion.
His right limbs all in proportion,
All twelve limbs equally balanced.
Not satisfied by begging food,
Never abandoning his greed,
Finding words when taken unawares,
Finding sight in darkness,
When driven into darkness,
Prowling like a lion—
Offspring of the noble Kyrgyz.
All is well with him.
By his nature the boy is exceptional,
A lion taking after his father.”
Pleased, saying this,
The wrestlers praised him.
Taytoru's many prizes,
The wrestlers shared them out.
All the wrestlers,
Their hearts lay calm as ashes.
In the city of Bukhara,
All the wrestlers
Were wealthy among the whole people.
Growing up as an orphan,
Thus joining the ranks,
All misfortunes scattered away,
His fortune opened like the sun,
Temir Khan in Bukhara
Gave a stern command.
His father's sovereignty,
At twelve, Semetey
Took wholly into his hands.
When his son mounted the throne,
Sparing nothing he possessed,
He gave a stern command.
The eight khans who came to Bukhara,
He gathered every one, leaving none out.
“Baabedin!” he shouted.
Unable to contain his joy, the poor fellow
Called all his people.
His many thoughts would not fit in his breast.
When many people came together,
His grandfather Temir Khan,
His tears streamed in ten directions.
To the four corners of the world,
His wealth gave him the means.
To Temir Khan's city,
When his daughter came wandering,
This was the child he had raised.
If he did not see him for three days,
He languished with longing, pleading,
Devoting all his attention to him.
Semetey at twelve,
Moreover, Temir Khan
Held as dear as his faith.
When his son mounted the throne,
Unable to contain his joy, Temir Khan
Shouted fiercely.
The eight khans who came to Bukhara,
Gathering them all then,
He proclaimed to his people:
“My dear eight khans,
Now God has granted my wish.
This Semetey here
Has turned twelve this year!
When my son mounts the throne,
How could I begrudge my livestock?
Not merely my livestock—for my son,
How could I begrudge my life?
The golden throne beneath me,
How could I begrudge my seat?
This Semetey here—
Now God has granted my wish.
He has reached twelve years of age!
Let your white-bearded elders come.
By your father's grave, eight khans,
Every one of you come, leaving none behind!
Let your skilled spearmen come,
Let your merciless champions come,
Let your swift runners and heroes come,
Let your beks who find sound reasons come.
Let me tell my sorrow!
My father was a khan before me.
I became khan of Bukhara
At precisely sixteen years of age.
Taking a wife and keeping a household,
Hanging steel at the side of my home,
Governing the people,
I had twelve daughters in succession,
The thirteenth was Kanykey.
For many years I was khan;
For a son to savor life with,
My poor head longed.
Setting out from Bukhara,
I received a letter from the caliph.
In the desert of Mediyan,
Received a blessing from a prince,
Coming to Bukhara and praying,
I devoted my thoughts to this.
After thirteen daughters,
I had my son Ismayyl.
People, rejoice at my words!
This Semetey here,
Born of Ismayyl,
Is my very own grandson.
When my only one mounts the throne,
I shall not spare my life a hair's breadth.
My treasury of four kinds of livestock,
I shall not spare my beasts a hair's breadth.
I offer my golden throne as a prize.
I offer together with it
This city of mine, gated Bukhara.
Eight houses filled with treasure,
Let me hack their entrances open.
All the wealth I have stored,
Let me spend and scatter it.
If these prizes prove too little,
Offer the hoe-working Tajik people.
If these prizes are to be opened,
Cut my beard and offer me.
At this son's feast,
May I come to no good if I so much as grumble!
If I say this or that,
May I no longer be a Muslim!
Without a post to tie a horse,
May I pass away utterly bare.
If I make my command into two,
If I wriggle out and cause a quarrel,
May I never come to any good!
For the people, laughter and diversion,
Put on merry games.
